Q000746.stem: A service pages on-call whenever CPU exceeds 80%, even when customers see no impact. The team wants one page only when CPU is high AND p99 latency exceeds 1 second, while CPU alone should just create a ticket. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An anomaly detection band on CPU that pages when it breaks
Longer evaluation periods on the existing CPU alarm that pages
A metric math alarm on CPU plus latency with one combined threshold
A composite alarm (CPU AND latency) that pages

Q000746.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Composite alarms combine the states of existing alarms with AND/OR logic. Paging only on CPU AND latency ties pages to customer impact, while the CPU alarm alone can notify a ticketing topic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection: changes CPU thresholds but still pages without impact.
• Summing CPU percent and milliseconds: units don't combine meaningfully.
• Longer periods: delays pages but doesn't require impact.

Key takeaway: page on impact; send causes to lower-urgency channels.

Q000754.stem: An app writes JSON logs with a level field and a service field. The team wants an alarm when ERROR logs exceed 50 per minute for any single service, without code changes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Insights on the application's log group
A scheduled Logs Insights query every minute that emails results
A subscription filter to Lambda that calls PutMetricData on each event
A JSON metric filter with the service as a dimension, plus an alarm

Q000754.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metric filters can match JSON fields (for example, { $.level = "ERROR" }) and publish a metric with dimensions taken from log fields, such as service, so one alarm per service works without code changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled query: delayed and not an alarm.
• Lambda per event: custom code and cost.
• CloudTrail Insights: analyzes API activity, not app logs.

Key takeaway: count log patterns → metric filters (with dimensions).

Q000755.stem: Every week an operator stops non-production instances, snapshots their volumes, and records the IDs in a ticket, with a manager's approval first. The team wants this repeatable, auditable, and runnable on a schedule. Which fits?

choices.text: An Automation runbook with an approval step, run on a schedule
A shell script stored in S3 and run from a bastion host
A Run Command document executed manually each week
A State Manager association that keeps instances in a stopped state

Q000755.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks define multi-step workflows that call AWS APIs (stop instances, create snapshots), can include approval steps, record execution history, and can run on schedules (for example, via EventBridge Scheduler or Maintenance Windows).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Run Command manually: a single command, not a gated multi-step workflow.
• State Manager: enforces a state continuously; no approval.
• Bastion script: not auditable or managed.

Key takeaway: multi-step, approved, auditable operations → Automation runbooks.

Q000761.stem: A team wants ML-based detection of operational anomalies across Lambda, DynamoDB, and API Gateway, with related events grouped into insights and remediation suggestions, without building models. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor operational checks
CloudWatch anomaly detection on each metric
Amazon Lookout for Metrics with custom models
Amazon DevOps Guru

Q000761.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DevOps Guru analyzes metrics, events, and logs across supported resources, detects anomalous behavior, correlates related anomalies into insights, and suggests remediation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-metric anomaly detection: no cross-resource correlation or insights.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Lookout for Metrics: business metric anomalies you configure, not operational insights.

Key takeaway: correlated operational insights → DevOps Guru.

Q000765.stem: A 200 GiB database volume needs 10,000 IOPS and 500 MB/s. The team is on gp2 and would have to grow to 3.4 TiB to get the IOPS. What is the most cost-effective change?

choices.text: Grow the gp2 volume to 3.4 TiB for the IOPS
Move to io2 with 10,000 provisioned IOPS
Move to st1 for higher throughput per dollar
Move to gp3 and provision IOPS and throughput

Q000765.explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 decouples performance from size: you can provision 10,000 IOPS and 500 MB/s on 200 GiB at a lower price than gp2's size-based scaling or io2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Growing gp2: pays for 3.4 TiB of unneeded storage.
• io2: meets it but costs more than necessary.
• st1: HDD with low IOPS.

Key takeaway: performance without extra size → gp3.

Q000772.stem: EC2 web servers behind an ALB become overloaded during unpredictable traffic surges, and at night most sit idle. The team wants capacity to follow load automatically across AZs. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm that emails the team to add instances
An Auto Scaling group with target tracking
Scheduled resizing of each instance to a larger type at peak
A fixed fleet sized for the historical peak

Q000772.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An Auto Scaling group across AZs with target tracking (for example, on ALB requests per target or CPU) adds and removes instances automatically as load changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled resizing: surges are unpredictable, and resizing needs restarts.
• Fixed peak fleet: idle waste at night.
• Email alarms: manual and slow.

Key takeaway: elastic capacity → Auto Scaling group + target tracking.

Q000774.stem: A global site serves static assets and personalized API responses from us-east-1. Asian users see slow page loads. Which CloudFront setup improves both parts?

choices.text: Replicate the S3 bucket to Asia and keep API calls direct
Cache static assets at the edge; proxy the API over the AWS backbone
Use CloudFront only for static assets and send API calls directly to us-east-1
Cache everything, including personalized API responses, for 24 hours

Q000774.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches static content near viewers and also accelerates dynamic requests by terminating TLS at the edge and using AWS's network to the origin, with caching disabled or keyed appropriately for personalized responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Caching personalized responses: users would see others' data.
• Direct API calls: miss the connection and network optimizations.
• Bucket replication: helps static files only and adds cost.

Key takeaway: CloudFront helps static (caching) and dynamic (edge termination, backbone) traffic.

Q000779.stem: An app's /health endpoint returns 200 even when its database is down, so the ALB keeps routing traffic to broken targets. What should change?

choices.text: A higher unhealthy threshold to reduce flapping
Switching the target group to TCP health checks
A shorter health check interval on the existing endpoint
A health endpoint that checks critical dependencies

Q000779.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Load balancers stop routing to targets that fail health checks, so the check must reflect the target's ability to serve requests. Be careful: if a shared dependency fails, all targets fail together.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shorter interval: faster checks of a meaningless signal.
• TCP checks: even less meaningful.
• Higher threshold: makes detection slower.

Key takeaway: health checks must test what matters (but consider shared dependencies).

Q000787.stem: Daily snapshots of a 1 TB volume change about 5 GB per day. A team deletes the first snapshot to save money and worries later snapshots are now broken. What is true?

choices.text: Later snapshots stay restorable; only unreferenced blocks are removed
Each snapshot is a full 1 TB copy, so deleting one saves 1 TB
Snapshots store only metadata, so deletion has no effect
Later snapshots break, since each depends on the first full copy

Q000787.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS snapshots are incremental, but AWS manages block references so any snapshot can restore the full volume. Deleting a snapshot removes only blocks no other snapshot references.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Broken chain: AWS preserves the needed blocks.
• Full copies: snapshots store only changed blocks.
• Metadata only: snapshots store data blocks.

Key takeaway: incremental storage, independent restore.

Q000793.stem: The team needs monthly patched and hardened AMIs, tested automatically, shared with 15 accounts, and launch templates updated with the new AMI. Which service fits?

choices.text: Systems Manager Patch Manager on running instances
A CodeBuild project calling CreateImage
EC2 Image Builder
AWS Backup AMI copies

Q000793.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image Builder pipelines build, harden, test, and distribute AMIs on a schedule, including sharing with accounts and updating launch templates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Backup copies: copy existing AMIs; they don't build or test.
• Patch Manager: patches running instances, not images.
• CodeBuild: custom scripting of what Image Builder provides.

Key takeaway: golden AMIs → Image Builder.

Q000795.stem: The same three-tier environment must be created identically in dev, test, and prod, updated with a preview of changes, and torn down cleanly. Which approach fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules that create any resources found to be missing
AMI copies of each environment restored into the other accounts
Manual console creation from a written runbook for each environment
CloudFormation templates deployed as stacks, using change sets

Q000795.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation defines resources declaratively and manages them as stacks; change sets preview updates, and deleting a stack removes its resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual runbook: drift and errors.
• Config rules: evaluate compliance, not provisioning.
• AMI copies: cover instances only, not the whole environment.

Key takeaway: repeatable environments → IaC stacks.

Q000796.stem: A team wants to define infrastructure in TypeScript with loops, shared libraries, and unit tests, while still deploying through CloudFormation. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog
AWS Config rules
AWS CDK
AWS OpsWorks

Q000796.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The AWS CDK uses general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, and others) to define infrastructure, supports reusable constructs and unit tests, and synthesizes CloudFormation templates for deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Service Catalog: distributes approved products; not an authoring language.
• OpsWorks: Chef or Puppet configuration management.
• Config rules: compliance checks.

Key takeaway: code-first IaC on CloudFormation → CDK.

Q000801.stem: A network team owns a VPC in a central account and wants application accounts to launch instances into its subnets, while the network team keeps control of routing and NACLs. Which service fits?

choices.text: StackSets that recreate the VPC in every account
AWS RAM sharing of the subnets
Cross-account roles to launch in the network account
VPC peering to a VPC in each application account

Q000801.explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC sharing through AWS RAM lets participant accounts create resources in shared subnets, while the owner account keeps control of the VPC, routes, and NACLs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: separate VPCs; doesn't share subnets.
• StackSets: duplicates networks rather than sharing.
• Roles in the network account: resources would belong to the network account.

Key takeaway: shared subnets across accounts → RAM VPC sharing.

Q000804.stem: A company manages AWS, Azure, and on-premises VMware with one IaC tool and shared modules. It wants to keep one tool for new AWS work. Which is most appropriate, and what must the team manage?

choices.text: AWS CDK, which deploys to Azure without extra providers
OpsWorks, which manages infrastructure across providers
Terraform; the team must manage and lock state
CloudFormation, which provisions Azure resources natively

Q000804.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Terraform supports multiple providers with one workflow. Unlike CloudFormation, the team manages state (for example, a remote backend with locking) and its security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFormation: AWS resources (plus registry extensions); not a multi-cloud standard.
• CDK: synthesizes CloudFormation for AWS.
• OpsWorks: configuration management, not multi-cloud provisioning.

Key takeaway: multi-cloud IaC → Terraform, with state management.

Q000806.stem: IaC templates live in Git. Changes must be reviewed, tested in CI, and applied automatically when merged, and every infrastructure change must be traceable to a commit. Which practice is this?

choices.text: GitOps-style IaC with pull requests and CI/CD
Blue/green deployment of application code only
A canary release of the IaC files to production
Manual console changes documented after the fact

Q000806.explanation:
Why this is correct:
GitOps treats Git as the source of truth: pull requests review changes, CI validates them, and merges trigger automated application, so each change maps to a commit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual changes: no traceability.
• Blue/green: an application deployment strategy.
• Canary of IaC files: not a standard practice for infrastructure changes.

Key takeaway: Git as source of truth + automated apply.

Q000811.stem: The team wants Lambda to run whenever an EC2 instance changes state, a SaaS partner sends an event, or a nightly schedule fires, with filtering on event content. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SNS
Amazon SQS
AWS Step Functions
Amazon EventBridge

Q000811.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge receives AWS service events, SaaS partner events, and custom events, filters them with patterns, supports schedules, and routes to targets such as Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS: pub/sub messaging, with no native AWS service event bus or SaaS partner sources.
• SQS: a queue, not event routing.
• Step Functions: orchestration, not event ingestion.

Key takeaway: event routing from many sources → EventBridge.

Q000815.stem: Alarms for RDS, EC2, and Lambda issues should create tracked operational issues with context, related resources, suggested runbooks, and status, deduplicated, rather than scattered emails. Which capability fits?

choices.text: Systems Manager OpsCenter OpsItems
AWS Config rule notifications
SNS topics with email subscriptions
CloudWatch dashboards

Q000815.explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpsCenter creates OpsItems from alarms and events, with related resources, runbook suggestions, status tracking, and deduplication.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS email: no tracking or context.
• Dashboards: visualization, not issue tracking.
• Config notifications: compliance only.

Key takeaway: track operational issues → OpsCenter.

Q000819.stem: An account must enforce passwords of at least 14 characters with symbols, prevent reuse of the last 5, and expire them every 90 days for IAM users. Which control fits?

choices.text: An SCP requiring strong passwords
An AWS Config rule that resets weak passwords
IAM Identity Center MFA settings
An IAM account password policy

Q000819.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The IAM account password policy sets length, character requirements, reuse prevention, and expiration for IAM user passwords.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP: controls API permissions, not password rules.
• Config: can evaluate the policy but doesn't enforce passwords.
• Identity Center MFA: a different identity store and control.

Key takeaway: IAM user password rules → account password policy.

Q000820.stem: Security requires MFA for root and every console user, with phishing-resistant keys for administrators. Some admins want to share one security key. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: One virtual MFA app can be assigned to several users at once
MFA can be enabled for the root user only
Keys can be registered per user; each MFA device belongs to one identity
IAM MFA automatically satisfies Cognito app logins

Q000820.explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM supports virtual, FIDO security key, and hardware TOTP devices. An MFA device is assigned to one IAM identity (a user can have several devices), so admins shouldn't share one device.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One device for several users: not supported.
• Root only: IAM users can use MFA too.
• Cognito: separate user pools.

Key takeaway: one device per identity; prefer FIDO keys for admins.

Q000822.stem: The team wants continuous findings for any S3 bucket, KMS key, or IAM role that grants access to principals outside its AWS Organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: GuardDuty findings for unusual S3 API calls
Amazon Macie findings for publicly accessible buckets
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust
Trusted Advisor checks for S3 bucket permissions

Q000822.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Access Analyzer evaluates resource policies (S3, KMS, IAM role trust, and others) and reports access granted outside the chosen zone of trust, such as the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: limited checks, mainly public buckets.
• Macie: data classification (with some bucket posture), not cross-account policy analysis for keys and roles.
• GuardDuty: behavior, not policy analysis.

Key takeaway: external access via policies → Access Analyzer.

Q000825.stem: An admin assigns the 'ReadOnlyOps' permission set to a group for 30 accounts. What is created in each account, and how do users get access?

choices.text: A resource policy added to every resource in each account
An IAM role from the set; users assume it through the access portal
An SCP attached to each of the 30 accounts in the organization
An IAM user per group member, each with long-term access keys

Q000825.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center provisions an IAM role from the permission set in each assigned account. Users sign in to the access portal and get temporary credentials for that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users: Identity Center doesn't create users with keys.
• SCP: a separate Organizations feature.
• Resource policies: not how permission sets work.

Key takeaway: permission set → role per account → temporary credentials.

Q000826.stem: The team wants an automated weekly check across all accounts for root MFA, security groups open to the world, and exposed access keys, with Business Support. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector network reachability
AWS Trusted Advisor with organizational view
Amazon Detective
AWS Config manual rules

Q000826.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor security checks include root MFA, unrestricted security group ports, and exposed access keys. Business Support and higher unlock all checks, and organizational view aggregates results.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities and reachability of workloads.
• Config manual rules: would need custom setup for each check.
• Detective: investigation, not checks.

Key takeaway: broad baseline checks → Trusted Advisor.

Q000829.stem: Operations must see at a glance which S3 buckets hold confidential data, and access policies and backups should follow automatically from that classification. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A spreadsheet of classifications kept outside AWS
Classification tags that drive policies and automation
Bucket names that include confidential or public
Different storage classes for each sensitivity level

Q000829.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tags such as data-classification=confidential are machine-readable. IAM (tag-based conditions), AWS Backup (tag-based selection), and automation can act on them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Names: can't be changed easily, and policies can't rely on them well.
• Spreadsheet: disconnected from enforcement.
• Storage classes: about cost and access, not sensitivity.

Key takeaway: classification as tags enables automated controls.

Q000830.stem: An ACM certificate using DNS validation has been Pending validation for two days. The domain's DNS is hosted by a third party. What must be done, and what keeps renewals automatic?

choices.text: Add ACM's CNAME at the DNS host and keep it for renewals
Transfer the domain's DNS to Route 53 permanently
Approve the email ACM sends to the domain's WHOIS contact
Upload the private key from an existing CA to ACM

Q000830.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation requires creating the CNAME record ACM provides at whichever DNS provider hosts the zone. Leaving it in place lets ACM renew automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email: that's the email validation method.
• Private key upload: not part of issuance.
• Route 53: convenient but not required.

Key takeaway: DNS validation = CNAME, kept in place.

Q000833.stem: Operations wants GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config findings in one normalized view across 20 accounts, with scores against AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Security Hub
Amazon Security Lake

Q000833.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings (ASFF) from services such as GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config, and runs security standards such as FSBP with scores, across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detective: investigation of findings.
• Audit Manager: evidence for audits.
• Security Lake: a data lake of logs for analytics, not a findings dashboard with standard scores.

Key takeaway: one findings view + standard scores → Security Hub.

Q000834.stem: A team wants to know which EC2 instances have critical CVEs AND are reachable from the internet, to fix those first. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
VPC Flow Logs analysis
Amazon Inspector (CVEs with network reachability)
AWS Trusted Advisor

Q000834.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and evaluates network reachability, factoring exposure into its risk score so internet-reachable critical findings rank highest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty: threat detection.
• Trusted Advisor: open ports checks, but no CVEs.
• Flow logs: traffic, not vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: prioritize vulnerabilities by exposure → Inspector.

Q000836.stem: Instances must be blocked from resolving known malware domains using an AWS-managed list, and blocked queries must be logged. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Security groups that deny outbound port 53
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with query logging
A private hosted zone containing each malicious domain
GuardDuty findings acting as the blocking control

Q000836.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall filters queries at the VPC resolver using managed or custom domain lists with BLOCK actions, and Resolver query logging records the queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG on port 53: would break all DNS.
• Private zones for bad domains: can't keep up with changing lists and isn't a policy tool.
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't block.

Key takeaway: domain blocking at the resolver → DNS Firewall.

Q000838.stem: Two EC2-based endpoints must receive DNS traffic 70/30 for an A/B test, and an endpoint should be removed from answers if its health check fails. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Multivalue answer records for both endpoints
Latency records for both endpoints
Failover records with the 30% endpoint as secondary
Weighted records (70/30) with health checks

Q000838.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing returns records in proportion to their weights, and associated health checks exclude unhealthy endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: routes by network performance, not proportions.
• Failover: all traffic to the primary until it fails.
• Multivalue: returns several healthy records but no set proportions.

Key takeaway: traffic percentages in DNS → weighted records.

Q000841.stem: After an incident, security needs to know which instances looked up a suspicious domain last week, with the source IP and response. Which log source fits?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver query logs
CloudTrail management events
VPC Flow Logs
ALB access logs

Q000841.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver query logging records DNS queries made from VPC resources, including the query name, source IP, instance ID where available, and response code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: exclude traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver.
• CloudTrail: AWS API calls, not DNS lookups.
• ALB logs: HTTP requests to the load balancer.

Key takeaway: who resolved what → Resolver query logs.

Q000844.stem: The zone apex example.com must point at a CloudFront distribution, and the company wants no charge for these queries and automatic tracking of CloudFront's IPs. Which record fits?

choices.text: A records containing CloudFront's current IPs
An MX record pointing to the distribution
A CNAME record at the apex pointing to CloudFront
Route 53 alias A/AAAA records to the distribution

Q000844.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alias records are allowed at the zone apex, follow the target's changing IPs, and queries to aliases for AWS resources such as CloudFront are free.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNAME at apex: not allowed by DNS rules.
• Hardcoded IPs: CloudFront IPs change.
• MX: mail routing.

Key takeaway: apex + AWS target → alias.

Q000846.stem: One instance in a public subnet with a public IPv4 address can't reach the internet, while others in the same subnet can. The subnet routes to an IGW. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the VPC has a peering connection to another VPC
Whether Shield Advanced is enabled on the account
Whether a gateway VPC endpoint was created for S3
Its SG, OS firewall, and routes; subnet-wide causes are ruled out

Q000846.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Because other instances in the same subnet work, the route table and NACL are likely fine. The difference is instance-specific: its security groups, OS firewall, OS routes, or a missing public IP association.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering, gateway endpoints, Shield: unrelated to one instance's internet access.

Key takeaway: compare what differs between working and failing instances.

Q000850.stem: Legitimate requests are being blocked by a web ACL. The team must identify which rule matched and see request details, then fix it without disabling the whole rule group. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Review VPC Flow Logs for the blocked requests
Check WAF logs; override that rule to Count
Check CloudTrail management events for WAF
Review Route 53 Resolver query logs

Q000850.explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF logs (and sampled requests) show the terminating rule and action for each request. A rule action override to Count for the specific managed rule stops blocking while the rest of the group stays active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: no HTTP detail.
• CloudTrail: API calls to configure WAF, not request evaluations.
• Resolver logs: DNS queries.

Key takeaway: find the rule in WAF logs; override narrowly.
